On 12 May Mrs Hoffmann turns 91. Mara and Lena are sitting in the bakery after closing time, looking for a present idea.
Next week Mrs Hoffmann is celebrating her birthday. We need a nice present. But what do you give a woman who's turning ninety-one?
Maybe a warm blanket? She always sits at the open window, and it's still chilly in the evenings.
A blanket is practical, but not very special. I'd like something with a little story behind it.
Hm. She has an old record player in her living room. But I've never seen a single record.
Grandpa told me she recorded her own record in the sixties. Chopin. But she doesn't have a single copy any more. They all got lost in a move.
Really? Then let's look for that record! After all, there are so many record shops in Berlin.
And at the flea market in the Mauerpark. And online. That's a great idea!
And what if we don't find it?
Then I'll bake a big cake and you'll buy a colourful bunch of flowers. And the warm blanket.
What kind of cake? She always says she doesn't like sweet things.
That's what she says. But every Monday she buys a big piece of Black Forest gateau from me. With extra cream.

1. The adjective after ein / kein / mein

The problem: “ein” is the same for masculine and neuter (ein Mantel, ein Kleid). How do you know the gender? The ADJECTIVE shows it, taking the ending of the definite article: der → ein neuER, das → ein neuES.
The differences from chapter 18 are just three boxes: masculine nominative (-er), neuter nominative and accusative (-es). Everything else is the same: -e or -en.
I don't have a warm coat.
When there's no article at all (with uncountable nouns, in the plural or after numbers), the adjective takes on the endings of the definite article by itself:

The golden rule: somewhere, either in the article or in the adjective, the “signal” of gender and case has to appear (-r, -s, -e, -m, -n). If the article already shows it (der, dem), the adjective only gets -e / -en. If there's no article, or it doesn't show it (ein), the adjective shows it.
Don't try to learn all the tables by heart at once. Learn one phrase from each: “der neue Kollege”, “ein neuer Kollege”, “mit freundlichen Grüßen” (kind regards, at the end of a letter).

Searching for the record was harder than Mara and Lena had thought. In the first record shop in Kreuzberg, a young shop assistant with long hair laughed: “Classical music from the GDR? By a pianist? Nobody looks for that here.” In the second shop, a small, dark shop in Neukölln, there were thousands of old records, but only jazz and rock.

Online they found the name: “Margarete Hoffmann spielt Chopin. Nocturnes. Eterna, 1964.” Eterna was the big record label of the GDR. But the record couldn't be bought anywhere. Just one man from Dresden had written on a forum ten years ago that he owned a copy. His email address no longer worked.

On Sunday they went to the flea market in the Mauerpark, to the stall where Ludwig had found his yellow tram lamp in the autumn. The stallholder, a fat man with a grey beard and a red woolly hat, remembered Ludwig at once.
The old tram driver! He didn't even haggle. You don't forget a customer like that. What are you looking for?
An old record. Eterna, 1964. Chopin, played by Margarete Hoffmann.

The stallholder scratched his beard. “I've got lots of Eterna. Crates full. My brother brings them from old flats in the East. People throw everything away when grandma dies.” He pointed to three big wooden crates under the table. “Have a look yourselves. If you find it, you can have it for five euros. For the tram driver.”

They searched for a whole hour. The records were dusty and smelled of old cellars. There was Russian folk music, pop hits from the seventies, politicians' speeches, children's stories, Beethoven, Bach, a children's choir from Leipzig. Mara's hands were black with dust. Lena had already sneezed three times.

In the third crate, right at the bottom, Mara found a record with a plain light blue cover. On it was a black-and-white photo: a young woman with black hair at the piano, her hands above the keys, her face serious and focused. Underneath, in simple white letters, it said: “Margarete Hoffmann · Frédéric Chopin · Nocturnes”.
Lena. Lena! I've got it! I found it!

The record was in surprisingly good condition. The cover had a small tear in the corner, but the black disc inside shone like new. On the back was a short text about the young pianist from Berlin, “a great hope of German piano music”.

Lena shrieked so loudly that people at the other stalls turned round. The stallholder took the record, looked at it for a long time and handed it back to them. “You can have this one for free,” he said. “But next Sunday you tell me what the old lady said.”

On the twelfth of May, at four in the afternoon, the whole building was standing on the fourth floor outside Mrs Hoffmann's door: Ludwig with his guitar, Lena with a big Black Forest gateau and ninety-one little candles, the Nowak family with a colourful bunch of flowers, Mara with a warm grey blanket and a flat parcel in red paper. Fritz was wearing a bow round his neck, which he didn't like at all.

They sang “Happy Birthday” in German, Polish and Romanian all at once, which sounded terrible and wonderful. Mrs Hoffmann stood in the doorway in her navy blue dress, laughing and scolding: “You're mad! I said I wasn't celebrating my birthday any more!” But she had made coffee for ten people and put ten cups on the table.

She opened the presents slowly, one after the other. She thanked them politely for the blanket. She was very pleased with the flowers. She had the cake cut straight away, “just a small piece, because of the sugar”, and then took a second one. Then Mara gave her the flat red parcel.

Mrs Hoffmann opened the paper. She saw the light blue cover. She saw the young woman at the piano. For a long time she said nothing. Her hands, her thin old hands with their long fingers, were trembling a little. Then she whispered: “Where did you get this? I haven't seen it for thirty years. I thought it didn't exist any more.”
Margarete, put it on. Please. I want to hear you play, like in the old days.

The old record player still worked. It crackled, it hissed, and then the little living room filled with music, with a slow, sad and wonderful nocturne, played by a young woman more than sixty years ago. The old lady sat beside it, in her warm new blanket, and listened to herself with her eyes closed.

When the side of the record had finished, she opened her eyes and looked at Mara. “You know, my child,” she said, “this is the most beautiful present I've had in many years. Not because of the record. Because of the people who looked for it.”

The following Sunday, Mara and Lena went back to the flea market and told the stallholder with the grey beard everything. He listened without saying a word. At the end he blew his nose on a big checked handkerchief and muttered: “Dust. It's just the dust from the old records.”
